title: Implement Bubble Sort — compare adjacent elements, swap if wrong order, repeat until sorted; O(n²) but easy to understand.

s1_definition.profdef: Bubble sort is a simple comparison-based sorting algorithm that repeatedly steps through the list, compares each pair of adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. After each full pass the largest remaining element has bubbled up to its final position at the end. It has quadratic time complexity in the worst and average cases, constant extra space, and is stable. An early-exit optimisation stops once a pass makes no swaps.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India arranging a row of account balances written on cards. The clerk compares the first two cards; if the left one is bigger, she swaps them. Then she compares the second and third, swapping if needed, and keeps moving right. After one full sweep, the largest balance has drifted all the way to the far right, like a bubble rising to the top. She repeats the sweeps, and each time the next-largest settles into place, until the whole row is sorted.
s1_definition.oneliner: Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs so the largest value bubbles to the end each pass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Bubble sort is a simple comparison-based sorting algorithm that repeatedly steps through the list, compares each pair of adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. After each full pass the largest remaining element has bubbled up to its final position at the end. It has quadratic time complexity in the worst and average cases, constant extra space, and is stable. An early-exit optimisation stops once a pass makes no swaps.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India arranging a row of account balances written on cards. The clerk compares the first two cards; if the left one is bigger, she swaps them. Then she compares the second and third, swapping if needed, and keeps moving right. After one full sweep, the largest balance has drifted all the way to the far right, like a bubble rising to the top. She repeats the sweeps, and each time the next-largest settles into place, until the whole row is sorted.

**One line to remember:** Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs so the largest value bubbles to the end each pass.

sections.s2_technical:
Bubble sort uses two nested loops. The outer loop counts the passes, and the inner loop walks adjacent pairs comparing and swapping. After the first pass the biggest element is parked at the last index, after the second pass the second biggest is parked just before it, and so on, so the inner loop can shrink by one each pass because the tail is already sorted.

The comparison uses the ordering rule. For BigDecimal balances we write `if (arr[j].compareTo(arr[j + 1]) > 0) swap(arr, j, j + 1);` which swaps when the left element is larger than its right neighbour, producing ascending order. The swap exchanges the two values using a temporary variable.

The key optimisation is a swapped flag. If an entire inner pass completes without a single swap, the array is already sorted and we break out early. This makes bubble sort run in linear time on data that is already sorted or nearly sorted, which is its one redeeming performance case. Without this flag it always does the full quadratic work.

A senior-level point is honesty about when to use it. Bubble sort's quadratic time makes it unsuitable for large datasets; sorting a million balances would be hopelessly slow compared to the library sort. It is valuable precisely because it is the clearest illustration of comparison and swapping, making it a teaching tool. It is stable, meaning equal elements keep their order, and it sorts in place using only constant extra memory. In real banking code I would never ship bubble sort; I use it only to explain the mechanics of sorting.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A junior developer at the National Bank of India is learning how sorting works and needs to see, step by step, how a small list of account balances gets ordered from smallest to largest. Bubble sort is perfect for this because every comparison and swap is visible and easy to follow, making it the clearest teaching example even though it is slow.

Problem 2 — Sometimes the balances arrive already nearly in order, for example a list that was sorted yesterday with one new entry appended. We want the algorithm to recognise this quickly rather than grinding through unnecessary passes. The swapped-flag optimisation lets bubble sort finish in a single pass when the data is already sorted.

In our mini-project we build a `BubbleSorter` that sorts an array of BigDecimal balances ascending, logging each swap and each pass, and uses the early-exit optimisation. The demo sorts a small unsorted array of the bank's balances and shows the pass-by-pass progress.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the array 1000000, 250000, 50000, 300000.

Step 1: Pass one begins. Compare 1000000 and 250000; left is bigger, so swap, giving 250000, 1000000, 50000, 300000.

Step 2: Compare 1000000 and 50000; swap, giving 250000, 50000, 1000000, 300000. Compare 1000000 and 300000; swap, giving 250000, 50000, 300000, 1000000. The largest value 1000000 has bubbled to the last position.

Step 3: Pass two works on the first three elements only, since the tail is sorted. Compare 250000 and 50000; swap, giving 50000, 250000, 300000, 1000000. Compare 250000 and 300000; no swap. Now 300000 is settled in the third position.

Step 4: Pass three works on the first two elements. Compare 50000 and 250000; no swap. No swaps occurred this pass.

Step 5: Because the swapped flag stayed false, the algorithm recognises the array is fully sorted and exits early rather than doing further passes.

Step 6: The final array is 50000, 250000, 300000, 1000000, sorted ascending in place with no extra memory.

```
[2026-10-26 20:40:03] INFO    Before: [1000000, 250000, 50000, 300000]
[2026-10-26 20:40:03] INFO    After pass 1: [250000, 50000, 300000, 1000000]
[2026-10-26 20:40:03] INFO    After pass 2: [50000, 250000, 300000, 1000000]
[2026-10-26 20:40:03] INFO    After pass 3: [50000, 250000, 300000, 1000000]
[2026-10-26 20:40:03] INFO    No swaps this pass — array is sorted, exiting early.
[2026-10-26 20:40:03] INFO    After:  [50000, 250000, 300000, 1000000]
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Bubble Sort ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  In-place swap with temp variable                             │
  │  Early-exit flag: break when a pass makes zero swaps          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: BubbleSorter only sorts                                  │

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             BubbleSorter              │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + sortAscending(arr): void           │  O(n²), O(1) space, stable
  │  - swap(arr, i, j): void              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      best case O(n) when already sorted (early exit)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. sortAscending(arr) → outer pass loop
  2. inner loop compare adjacent, swap if left>right
  3. after pass with no swaps → break (sorted)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Bubble sort is a simple comparison-based algorithm that repeatedly steps through the list, compares each pair of adjacent elements, and swaps them when they are in the wrong order. After each full pass the largest remaining element has bubbled up to its correct position at the end, so I can shrink the inner loop by one on every subsequent pass because the tail is already sorted. It has quadratic time in the average and worst cases, uses only constant extra memory, and is stable.

The one optimisation I always include is a swapped flag. If an entire pass completes without a single swap, the array is already sorted and I break out early. That turns bubble sort into linear time on already-sorted or nearly-sorted data, which is its single redeeming performance case.

In my banking context at the National Bank of India I use bubble sort purely as a teaching tool. When a junior developer is learning how sorting works, bubble sort makes every comparison and swap visible, so I can walk them through how a list of account balances gets ordered step by step. I log each pass so they can watch the largest balance drift to the end each time.

The senior-level point I am always honest about is that I would never ship bubble sort in production. Its quadratic time makes it hopeless for large datasets; sorting a million balances would be unbearably slow next to the library sort. Its value is entirely educational and it illustrates the core idea of comparison-and-swap more clearly than any other algorithm. For real work I use Java's highly optimised stable TimSort, and I reserve bubble sort for explaining the fundamentals.

keyPoints: Comparison sorts: merge sort O(n log n), quick sort O(n log n) average
Non-comparison: counting sort, radix sort — O(n) for limited range
Kth largest: quickselect O(n) average, heap O(n log k)
